questions.text: Why is the Bahay Kubo a key vernacular anchor?

options.text: It is identified as a passively cooled lowland dwelling with porous surfaces, horizontal windows, overhangs, gardens, and light local materials.

questions.rationale: It is identified as a passively cooled lowland dwelling with porous surfaces, horizontal windows, overhangs, gardens, and light local materials. HOA Module 4 P1 and Filipino Architecture describe the Bahay Kubo as climate-responsive and materially light.
questions.explanation: Pagtatali (lashing) is the defining structural technique of pre-colonial bahay kubo construction. Rattan, abaca fiber, or bamboo strips are wrapped tightly around joints between haligi (posts), batangan (joists), and other members. Unlike rigid metal connections, lashing allows the joint to flex under earthquake or typhoon loading — the connection can stretch and return to shape rather than snapping. This is why traditional bahay kubo structures have survived centuries of Philippine typhoons and earthquakes without catastrophic collapse. Metal fasteners (nails, bolts) only appeared with Spanish and later American colonial influence.

questions.explanation: The HALIGI ng BAHAY mnemonic encodes the vertical structural path of the bahay kubo from bottom to top: Haligi (main posts driven into ground or resting on stones/tukod) carry the Batangan (horizontal floor joists/girders), which carry the Sahig (split bamboo floor slats). The Dingding (woven bamboo/nipa walls) enclose the space, and the Bubong (steeply pitched nipa/cogon/buri thatch roof) provides weather protection. The chant 'Haligi, Batangan, Sahig, Dingding, Bubong' makes this sequence memorable. Critically, the load travels downward through this path: roof → walls → floor → joists → posts → ground.

questions.explanation: Bundled bamboo is one of four joinery/construction techniques in bahay kubo construction: (1) Pagtatali (lashing) — rattan/abaca strips around joints; primary technique for flexibility; (2) Mortise-and-tenon — interlocking hardwood carved joints for compression strength; (3) Wedge/peg joints — bamboo or hardwood pegs through drilled holes; shear resistance with flexibility; (4) Bundled bamboo — multiple culms grouped and lashed at joints to create composite members thicker and stronger than any single culm. Bundled bamboo is particularly used for haligi (main posts) and batangan (main joists) where single culms would be insufficient in larger structures.

questions.explanation: The S-B-B-K mnemonic describes the spatial organization of the bahay kubo as you move from front to back: (1) Silong — the open space under the elevated floor, visible from the entrance; (2) Bulwagan — the main open living hall at the center; (3) Silid — the partitioned sleeping area; (4) Batalan — the back porch/service area for washing and water storage (with tapayan/water jars); (5) Kusina — the kitchen, often in a separate extension with an abuhan (clay stove). Note the doubled B: Bulwagan and Batalan, both starting with B.

questions.explanation: The hagabi is a disc-shaped wooden or bamboo element fitted around the posts of the Ifugao bale (and other Cordillera dwellings) to prevent rats from climbing up the posts and into the grain stores and living space. It is both a functional pest-control device and a cultural artifact — the shape and carving of hagabi vary among Ifugao clans. The bale itself is a compact, single-room dwelling elevated on four main posts, with a pyramidal thatched roof.

questions.explanation: Every element of the bahay kubo is a direct response to the Philippine tropical monsoon climate: (1) RAISED FLOOR: Elevates living space above flood level; creates the silong (ventilated under-floor space); the batangan (joists) carry the sahig (floor slats) with gaps that allow air to flow through the floor from the silong into the living area; (2) STEEP ROOF (45–60°): The bubong of nipa/cogon/buri is steeply pitched to shed the heavy monsoon rains quickly; (3) OPEN WALLS: The dingding (woven bamboo/sawali walls) and bintana (sliding bamboo panels) can be opened entirely for maximum ventilation. The house is oriented to catch prevailing monsoon winds — long axis perpendicular to the dominant wind to maximize cross-ventilation.

questions.explanation: The bahay kubo evolved into the bahay na bato gradually: (1) Pre-colonial (pre-1565): Pure bahay kubo — all-organic materials, raised floor, open silong; (2) Early Spanish (16th–17th c.): Introduction of stone or brick to replace wooden posts at ground level — improving durability and fire resistance while keeping the raised floor; (3) Mature Spanish (18th–19th c.): Full bahay na bato emerges — enclosed stone ground floor (zaguan/silung), wooden upper floor with sala/cuartos/volada, capiz-shell windows (ventanillas), clay tile or GI sheet roofing. The indigenous raised-floor logic was preserved; only the materials and enclosure of the ground level changed.

questions.explanation: The torogan is one of the most architecturally distinguished indigenous dwellings in the Philippines. Key features: (1) Okir carvings — elaborate geometric designs carved into posts, beams, and panels; okir is a Maranao art form with Islamic geometric roots; (2) High-peaked roof — dramatically steep, often described as the highest of all Philippine indigenous roof forms; (3) Raised on massive logs — the structure is elevated on thick hardwood posts; (4) No interior partitions — a single large open hall reflecting the communal nature of Maranao royal households. It is NOT a bahay kubo variant — it is a distinct royal typology of the Maranao people.
